messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Jacobian adjustments...
parts:
Given the following, where I want to put a prior on on a) the mean of a set of parameters, and b) the relation between various transformations of parameters, the need for jacobian adjustment is not clear to me. I appreciate that much has been written on this general topic here in the past, and there are many cases where it is clear to me thanks to such... but I somehow find these two elusive! any help would be very appreciated. 

This is an incomplete toy problem that attempts to represent the issues - if I just want to encode my knowledge about the expected mean of y, and it's relation to some transformation of x, is there some way the jacobian should be adjusted? At present I think not, but can't convince myself either way...

data{
vec[z] mydata[n]
}
parameters{
vec[n] y;
real x;
}
model{

mean(y) ~ normal(0, 1) ;
mean(y) / x^2 ~ normal(1, 0.1);

for(i in 1:n){
mydata[i] ~ normal(y[i],x)
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Jacobian adjustments...
parts:
Overall, I'd urge you to think more generatively in
terms of generating the parameters from priors and the data
from the parameters. See below.

> On Oct 10, 2016, at 6:24 AM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Given the following, where I want to put a prior on on a) the mean of a set of parameters, and b) the relation between various transformations of parameters,
> the need for jacobian adjustment is not clear to me. I appreciate that much has been written on this general topic here in the past, and there are many cases where it is clear to me thanks to such... but I somehow find these two elusive! any help would be very appreciated.

It's elusive because it's not a typical generative model!
Usually when we transform parameters and put a prior on
the transform, we're really thinking of things the other way
around in more generative terms and just using the transform
for convenience.

> This is an incomplete toy problem that attempts to represent the issues - if I just want to encode my knowledge about the expected mean of y, and it's relation to some transformation of x, is there some way the jacobian should be adjusted? At present I think not, but can't convince myself either way...
>
> data{
> vec[z] mydata[n]
> }
> parameters{
> vec[n] y;
> real x;
> }
> model{
>
> mean(y) ~ normal(0, 1) ;

You probably don't want two priors on the same parameter y.
And putting a distribution on a sum isn't identified---see
the manual chapter on problematic posteriors for a simple
example of why.

In general, if

for (i in 1:n)
z[i] ~ normal(0, sigma);

then

sum(z) ~ normal(0, sqrt(n) * sigma);

and

sum(z) / n ~ normal(0, sqrt(n) * sigma / n);

and mean(z) = sum(z) / n, so you can take

y ~ normal(0, sqrt(n));

and you will get

mean(y) ~ normal(0, 1)

as a consequence. But this is *not* the same thing as
just writing the statement for the mean. That statement
for the mean gives y[1] = 1e20 and y[2] = -1e20 and
y[1] = 1 and y[2] = -1 the same probability, which probably
isn't what you want.

I didn't understand why you'd want to do this.
What exactly are you trying to accomplish with these two
priors on y? In Stan terms, the densities just multiply.

For efficiency, this should just be

mydata ~ normal(y, x);

- Bob

P.S. We like to use y for modeled data, x for predictors,
and lower case n for loop indices and capital N for sizes,
then loop for (n in 1:N) so that the index matches the bound
so it's less things to remember when trying to read the code.

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Jacobian adjustments...
parts:
Thanks for your thoughts Bob. Yes I thought the 'not generative' aspect was probably the issue confusing things. The context for this is multivariate stochastic processes, where I think it probably makes some sense, at least as a pragmatic decision... as while on the one hand I want to be able to define the processes in terms of partial differential matrices, on the other I also want to be able to impose some tendency on the asymptotic behaviour - that is I want to push the diagonals of the initial covariance matrix and the asymptotic covariance matrix (a matrix of transformed parameters) towards equivalence. I understand your point re a nonidentified distribution on a sum, in general I *would* actually put two priors on the parameters, as I would also handle the log sd in the same manner - though in both cases I would also include a separate, freely sampled term for the disturbance from mean(y) or logsd(y). This creates some form of a non-centered distribution but with the lower level parameters as fundamental, I posted something similar before but understand it a little better now. Because that was probably unclear:

data{
vec [T] y[N];
}
parameters{
vec mu[N];
real hypermean_disturbance;
real hyperlogsd_disturbance;
}
transformed parameters{
real hypermean;
real hyperlogsd;
hypermean <- mean(mu) + hypermean_disturbance;
hyperlogsd <- log(sd(mu)) + hyperlogsd_disturbance;
}
model{
mu~normal(hypermean,exp(hyperlogsd));
hypermean ~ normal(0,10);
hyperlogsd ~ normal(0,10);
for(n in 1:N){
Y[n] ~ normal(mu[n], someothersdparameter);

}
}

I didn't see a question in there, but the model you append looks
like a generative model, it's not a well-formed Stan program
(variable "someothersdparameter" not declared).

I meant putting two priors on the same parameter, as you were
suggesting in the last post. Stan lets you write:

mu ~ normal(0, 1);
mu ~ noraml(1, 3);

if you want, and the density is

p(mu) propto normal(mu | 0, 1) * normal(mu | 1, 3)

- Bob
